Genetic Diversity in Populations

Chapter 19: build the normal mechanisms, practise with support, and use the biology to explain a new case.

How to use this chapter

Work through the lessons in order. Each lesson explains the idea, shows a worked example and gives you practice before the lesson check.

Everything needed for the lesson checks is taught here. Videos and the embedded textbook are optional support.

Try each question before checking feedback. When you make a correction, explain what changed in your thinking. Saved work and corrected choices help you track progress, but completing an activity does not by itself prove understanding.

What you will learn

  • Calculate allele and genotype frequencies with the correct denominators.
  • Use Hardy–Weinberg as an explicit reference model rather than an automatic assumption.
  • Distinguish selection, drift, gene flow and mutation.
  • Evaluate genetic and demographic evidence in population cases.

Start with the lesson

The explanations, figures and worked examples teach the biology here. The textbook and videos provide optional support.

Each teaching lesson has two selections and two written explanations in its required check. The final check has six selections and two written explanations. Save each written response, then submit and finish the run. Writing is saved for review, not automatically graded.

Populations, gene pools and genetic variation

What changes when a population evolves?

Learning goal

Define a gene pool and distinguish change in a population from change within an individual.

Before you begin

Individuals carry alleles. Inheritance passes alleles between generations, while population size can also change.

Chapter 19 · printed pp. 678–679

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

Individuals of the same species occupying a defined area during a defined time.
All the alleles present in the reproductive population being considered.
Differences in genetic information among individuals or lineages.
A change in allele frequencies in a population across generations.

Define the population you are studying

genetics studies the genetic composition of populations and how that composition changes. A population consists of individuals of the same species within a defined place and time. Those boundaries matter: counting one breeding colony is not the same as counting every colony across a continent.

The is the collection of alleles present in that population. An individual carries only part of the population’s variation. At an ordinary diploid autosomal locus, each individual contributes two allele copies.

Track proportions across generations

is a change in allele frequencies across generations. An allele frequency is its share of all allele copies at the locus. It is a proportion, not simply the number of individuals showing a trait.

Suppose a population doubles in size while every allele’s proportion stays the same. The number of copies increases, but the allele frequencies have not changed. Conversely, frequencies can change even if the total population size remains constant.

An individual’s body can grow, develop or adjust to conditions. Those changes are not themselves evidence that a population’s inherited allele frequencies have changed.

Distinguish genetic and environmental differences

can influence phenotypes, but environment and gene regulation also matter. A plant grown in shade may differ from a genetically similar plant grown in bright light. That observation alone does not identify an allele-frequency change.

To study evolution at a locus, specify the alleles and measure or infer their frequencies with appropriate evidence. Later lessons explain when genotype counts permit direct counting and when a mathematical model is required.

Do not assume every genetic difference is advantageous, or that evolution always moves toward greater size or complexity. The mechanisms can include selection and chance.

Worked example

Count change versus frequency change

A population grows from 100 to 200 diploid individuals. Allele A rises from 60 of 200 copies to 120 of 400 copies.

  1. At the first sampling, A frequency is 60/200 = 0.30.
  2. At the second, it is 120/400 = 0.30.
  3. The number of A copies doubled but its proportion did not.
  4. These measurements show no allele-frequency change at this locus over the interval.

Practise with support

Apply the explanation

Try both questions. Use the hint to revise your thinking after an incorrect answer.

Stop and think

Try this before opening the explanation

Show the explanation

Yes. The composition can change even when the total number does not.

Allele frequencies and genotype frequencies

Why do allele calculations usually use twice as many copies as individuals?

Chapter 19 · printed pp. 679–682

Open p. 679 · Open p. 682

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

The proportion of individuals with a specified genotype.
The proportion of allele copies represented by a particular allele at a locus.
The contribution of one copy of each allele from a heterozygous individual.
The requirement that mutually exclusive complete categories account for the whole sample.

Count individuals for genotype frequencies

Let N be the number of diploid individuals sampled at a two-allele autosomal locus. The possible genotypes are AA, Aa and aa. is the number with one genotype divided by N.

For 30 AA, 50 Aa and 20 aa individuals, N = 100. The frequencies are 0.30, 0.50 and 0.20. They add to 1 because every sampled individual belongs to exactly one of these genotype categories.

Count copies for allele frequencies

The same sample contains 2N = 200 allele copies. Each AA contributes two A copies, each Aa contributes one A and one a, and each aa contributes two a copies.

The A count is 2(30) + 50 = 110, so p = 110/200 = 0.55. The a count is 2(20) + 50 = 90, so q = 90/200 = 0.45. The allele frequencies also add to 1.

The general relationships are p = [2(AA) + Aa]/2N and q = [2(aa) + Aa]/2N, where the genotype symbols inside the brackets represent counts. Write units or category names beside the numbers so that individuals are not mistaken for allele copies.

Direct counting does not need equilibrium

When all genotype counts are known, allele frequencies can be calculated directly. You do not need to assume Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium to count copies.

A recessive phenotype alone provides different information. Under a simple complete-dominance model, it identifies aa individuals but does not separate AA from Aa among dominant-phenotype individuals. Additional assumptions would be needed to infer all allele frequencies from that phenotype count alone.

Check every calculation: genotype counts total N, allele counts total 2N, and both sets of frequencies separately sum to 1.

Worked example

Use all genotype counts

A sample has 40 AA, 40 Aa and 20 aa individuals. Find p and q.

  1. Total individuals N = 100; total allele copies = 200.
  2. A copies = 2(40) + 40 = 120, so p = 120/200 = 0.60.
  3. a copies = 2(20) + 40 = 80, so q = 80/200 = 0.40.
  4. Check: 0.60 + 0.40 = 1.
  5. These are direct counts, not an inference from equilibrium.

Practise with support

Apply the explanation

Try both questions. Use the hint to revise your thinking after an incorrect answer.

Stop and think

Try this before opening the explanation

Can the dominant phenotype always distinguish AA from Aa?

Show the explanation

No. Under complete dominance, both can have the same phenotype.

What does a non-evolving reference model allow us to predict?

Learning goal

Chapter 19 · printed pp. 681–684

Open p. 681 · Open p. 684

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

A model in which allele frequencies remain constant and genotype frequencies follow p², 2pq and q² under stated conditions.
Mating that is independent of the genotype being considered.
The expected frequency of one homozygous genotype under a two-allele Hardy–Weinberg model.
The expected heterozygote frequency under the two-allele Hardy–Weinberg model.

Start with the allele pool

At a locus with two alleles, let p be the frequency of A and q the frequency of a. Because these are the complete allele categories, p + q = 1. This identity does not require equilibrium.

If gametes combine randomly with those frequencies, AA has expected frequency p × p = p² and aa has q × q = q². A heterozygote can arise as A from one gamete and a from the other, or the reverse. Its total expected frequency is pq + qp = .

Name the conditions rather than hiding them

The Hardy–Weinberg reference model assumes a very large , with respect to the locus, no mutation, no migration and no natural selection affecting the alleles or genotypes. A very large population minimizes chance fluctuations from sampling.

Under these idealized conditions, allele frequencies remain constant across generations and genotype proportions follow p² + 2pq + q² = 1. The model gives a baseline for asking whether observed data fit the prediction.

A real population need not satisfy every condition perfectly. A mismatch can suggest that assumptions need investigation, but the mismatch alone does not identify which mechanism caused it.

Dominance is not the cause of frequency

The letters p and q can represent the two alleles whether or not one is dominant. In familiar complete-dominance problems, p often names the dominant allele and q the recessive allele. This notation does not make p larger than q.

Dominance determines the heterozygote’s phenotype. It does not determine the allele’s frequency or guarantee that the dominant allele is favoured by selection.

When only the recessive phenotype count is given, identifying q² and taking its square root requires the stated equilibrium and phenotype-model assumptions. Without them, do not silently infer the unobserved genotypes.

Worked example

Derive a heterozygote prediction

At a two-allele locus, p = 0.70 and q = 0.30. Assume Hardy–Weinberg conditions.

  1. AA expectation is 0.70 × 0.70 = 0.49.
  2. aa expectation is 0.30 × 0.30 = 0.09.
  3. Aa expectation is 2 × 0.70 × 0.30 = 0.42.
  4. Check: 0.49 + 0.42 + 0.09 = 1.
  5. These genotype predictions depend on the model, unlike the allele total p + q = 1.

Practise with support

Apply the explanation

Try both questions. Use the hint to revise your thinking after an incorrect answer.

Stop and think

Try this before opening the explanation

Does p² + 2pq + q² = 1 prove that a real population satisfies all five assumptions?

Show the explanation

No. A calculation using the formula is not evidence that the assumptions hold.

How do you move from a recessive phenotype count to expected carrier numbers?

Chapter 19 · printed pp. 683–688

Open p. 683 · Open p. 688

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

The expected aa genotype frequency under a two-allele Hardy–Weinberg model.
The proportion of heterozygotes carrying a recessive allele in the stated model.
A model-predicted number obtained by multiplying a frequency by population size.
Recovering q from q² when the Hardy–Weinberg assumptions apply.

Identify the given quantity

Suppose a recessive phenotype occurs in 32 of 200 individuals and the problem explicitly assumes with complete dominance. The observed aa fraction is 32/200 = 0.16, which is used as q².

Take the square root to obtain the recessive : q = √0.16 = 0.40. Then p = 1 − q = 0.60. Do not call 0.16 the allele frequency; it describes individuals with two recessive copies.

Predict genotypes and convert to counts

Use the allele frequencies to calculate the expected genotype frequencies: p² = 0.36, = 0.48 and q² = 0.16. These are the expected fractions of AA, Aa and aa individuals.

To obtain counts, multiply each frequency by N = 200. The expected numbers are 72 AA, 96 Aa and 32 aa. Check that the counts total 200 and the frequencies total 1.

The heterozygotes are carriers in this simple recessive model. The dominant-phenotype fraction includes AA and Aa together, so it is 0.36 + 0.48 = 0.84, not p alone.

Keep precision until the final answer

Carry sufficient decimal precision through square roots and multiplication. Round the final expected number to an appropriate whole individual only after completing the calculation. Rounding q too early can noticeably change a carrier estimate.

If allele frequency is already given, start with that value instead of taking another square root. If all genotype counts are given, direct allele counting may be the appropriate first method.

A strong answer states the model, labels each quantity, shows the calculation and interprets the result. A bare number makes it difficult to see whether the correct denominator and assumption were used.

Worked example

Estimate carriers for a rare recessive condition

In a hypothetical population at Hardy–Weinberg equilibrium, 1 in 10 000 individuals has a fully recessive phenotype.

  1. q² = 1/10 000 = 0.0001.
  2. q = √0.0001 = 0.01, so p = 0.99.
  3. Carrier frequency = 2pq = 2(0.99)(0.01) = 0.0198.
  4. As a percentage, this is 1.98%, not 0.0198%.
  5. The inference depends on the stated model; it is not a personal medical-risk estimate.

Practise with support

Apply the explanation

Try both questions. Use the hint to revise your thinking after an incorrect answer.

Stop and think

Try this before opening the explanation

Show the explanation

No. Take it when the given quantity is q² and the model justifies that interpretation.

Using population data to test a prediction

How can the same allele frequencies produce different genotype patterns?

Learning goal

Before you begin

Chapter 19 · printed pp. 685–688

Open p. 685 · Open p. 688

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

A count actually supplied or measured in the sample.
The genotype proportions predicted by the selected model.
Differences that arise because a finite sample does not reproduce population proportions perfectly.
Evaluation of how well observations fit a model’s predictions.

Calculate the observed allele pool first

Suppose a sample has 40 AA, 20 Aa and 40 aa individuals. There are 100 individuals and 200 allele copies. A copies total 80 + 20 = 100, so p = 0.50; q is also 0.50.

These allele frequencies are directly observed from genotype counts. Under Hardy–Weinberg, they predict 25 AA, 50 Aa and 25 aa individuals in a sample of 100. The observed sample contains fewer heterozygotes than that prediction.

A genotype mismatch is not a unique explanation

A shortage of heterozygotes could be associated with non-, structure or other processes. The counts alone do not uniquely establish which mechanism acted. Sampling and measurement also need consideration.

Notice that the observed sample and the predicted distribution have the same p and q. Genotype proportions can differ while allele frequencies remain the same. Non-random mating can alter genotype proportions without necessarily changing allele frequencies by itself.

Keep two questions separate: do genotype proportions fit the random-mating model, and have allele frequencies changed across generations? They require related but different comparisons.

Use consistent sampling and restrained conclusions

To compare generations, sample the same defined population and locus using comparable methods. A change in p or q supports allele-frequency change at that locus, but a different sampling location or age group can complicate interpretation.

Agreement with a prediction is not proof that every Hardy–Weinberg condition is perfectly satisfied. Opposing effects can sometimes balance, and finite samples have limited resolution. A visible mismatch is a reason to investigate, not permission to name a mechanism without evidence.

These activities use direct comparisons and arithmetic. Formal statistical testing may be useful in research, but no unsupported significance claim is needed here.

Worked example

Same alleles, different pairing

Population A has 25 AA, 50 Aa and 25 aa individuals. Population B has 50 AA, 0 Aa and 50 aa.

  1. Both populations have N = 100 and 200 allele copies.
  2. Both contain 100 A and 100 a copies, so p = q = 0.50.
  3. Population A matches the 1:2:1 genotype prediction for p = q = 0.50.
  4. Population B has the same allele frequencies but no heterozygotes.
  5. Allele totals alone do not establish random genotype pairing.

How do survival and mating success affect inherited variation?

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

Differential reproductive success associated with heritable variation in a particular environment.
Reproductive contribution compared with other genotypes or phenotypes in the relevant setting.
Selection associated with differences in mating success.
Mating patterns that depend on characteristics related to the genotype being studied.

Follow reproduction, not intention

Individuals vary, and some variation is heritable. If a heritable trait affects survival or reproduction, the associated alleles may be represented differently in the next generation. describes that differential reproductive contribution.

The environment matters. A trait advantageous in one setting may have little benefit or a cost elsewhere. Fitness therefore refers to contribution to future generations in context, not simply strength, speed or size.

Selection does not make an organism deliberately produce a needed mutation. Variation must exist or arise independently before its consequences can affect reproductive success.

Distinguish survival from mating success

A trait can increase survival but reduce mating opportunities, or increase mating success while imposing a survival cost. focuses on differences in obtaining mates and reproducing.

For example, a conspicuous display might attract mates while also increasing exposure to predators. The overall evolutionary effect depends on the balance of reproductive consequences, not on whether the display appears efficient to an observer.

A claim that selection occurred needs evidence relating heritable differences to reproductive outcomes. A change in frequency alone can also arise through chance or movement between populations.

Pairing patterns and allele totals are different

changes who pairs with whom. It can change genotype frequencies, such as increasing homozygosity, without directly changing allele frequencies if all alleles retain the same overall reproductive contribution.

Sexual selection and non- are related but not identical statements. When mating success differs, some individuals contribute more offspring. When only pairing patterns differ, allele totals need not immediately change.

Use the information in the case to identify what varies: pairing, survival, number of offspring, or several together.

Worked example

A mating advantage with a survival cost

A hypothetical heritable display makes males more visible to predators but substantially increases successful mating.

  1. The survival effect is a possible cost.
  2. The mating effect is a possible advantage.
  3. Assess overall reproductive contribution rather than judging only survival.
  4. If display-associated variants contribute more descendants, sexual selection can favour them.
  5. The conclusion depends on measured reproductive outcomes in the stated environment.

Chapter 19 · printed pp. 691–694

Open p. 691 · Open p. 694

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

Random change in allele frequencies caused by chance sampling in finite populations.
A change in genetic composition associated with a sharp reduction in population size.
A change in allele representation when a small subset establishes a new population.
An allele reaching frequency 1 at the locus in the population considered.

Chance can change the sample

Not every individual leaves the same number of descendants. In a finite , chance differences can change allele frequencies even when the alleles have no effect on survival or reproduction. This is .

Drift has a stronger relative effect in small populations because a small number of births, deaths or reproductive events can represent a large fraction of the . An allele may be lost or become fixed by chance.

A useful distinction is whether the case links reproductive success with a heritable trait. Trait-related differences support selection; random sampling independent of the trait supports drift. Both processes can operate together.

A bottleneck samples the original population

A bottleneck occurs when population size falls sharply. The survivors may carry a smaller and unrepresentative sample of the earlier alleles. If the reduction is random with respect to a studied allele, drift can strongly change that allele’s frequency.

If the population later increases, descendants reproduce the variation that survived. Recovery in numbers does not automatically bring back alleles that were lost. Mutation or gene flow might introduce variation later, but population growth alone does not guarantee restoration.

Founders establish a new gene pool

A occurs when a small group starts a new population. The founders may carry allele frequencies different from those of the source population simply because they are a small sample.

The source population can remain large and intact. That separates the founder case from a bottleneck that reduces an existing population. Both involve sampling, but the demographic history differs.

Do not infer that a newly common allele must be adaptive. A small island population can have unusual allele frequencies because of its founders even before evidence of local selection is available.

Worked example

Name the demographic event

Five individuals leave a large population to establish an isolated colony. By chance, they carry an uncommon allele at a high frequency.

  1. The original population remains large.
  2. The new population begins from a small sample of its allele pool.
  3. This is a founder effect, a form of genetic drift.
  4. No selective advantage is needed to explain the initial frequency difference.

Chapter 19 · printed pp. 694–697

Open p. 694 · Open p. 697

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

Transfer of alleles between populations through successful genetic contribution.
The introduction of new sequence variants through mutation.
The degree to which populations exchange genetic contributions.
Differences in genetic composition among populations.

Track successful contributions, not movement alone

transfers alleles between populations. It can occur when individuals migrate and reproduce, or when gametes such as pollen move between populations. The important event is a genetic contribution to the recipient .

An animal passing through a habitat without reproducing does not necessarily alter the next generation’s allele pool. Movement can create an opportunity, but successful reproduction connects that movement with inherited change.

Combine copies with the correct weights

Suppose 80 resident diploid breeders have A frequency 0.25 and 20 immigrant breeders have A frequency 0.75. If all contribute equally, residents supply 160 copies including 40 A; immigrants supply 40 copies including 30 A. The combined frequency is 70/200 = 0.35.

Do not take a simple average of 0.25 and 0.75 when the groups differ in size. Weight each frequency by the number of allele copies contributed. The equal-contribution assumption also matters: different reproductive success would change the weights.

Gene flow can add variation within a population and reduce genetic differences between populations, although the actual effect depends on their starting allele pools and contributions.

Mutation supplies new variants

Mutation changes DNA sequence and can create new alleles. A heritable mutation must enter the reproductive lineage to affect later generations. Many mutations have little effect in a particular setting; others can be harmful or beneficial.

Mutation and selection play different roles. Mutation generates sequence differences without knowing future need. Selection can favour or remove variants according to their reproductive consequences. Drift can also alter their frequencies, especially when a new variant is rare.

Isolation and habitat fragmentation can reduce opportunities for gene flow. A conservation argument about connectivity should therefore look for movement, successful reproduction and genetic evidence rather than assuming that a structure’s presence proves its effect.

Worked example

Weight two contributing groups

A recipient population has 60 breeders at p = 0.20. Forty immigrants have p = 0.70. Assume equal contribution per diploid breeder.

  1. Residents contribute 120 allele copies, including 24 A.
  2. Immigrants contribute 80 copies, including 56 A.
  3. Combined A copies = 80 of 200, so p = 0.40.
  4. The larger resident group receives the larger weight.
  5. The result predicts the combined contribution pool under the equal-contribution assumption.

Show the explanation

Chapter 19 · printed pp. 695–697

Open p. 695 · Open p. 697

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

The variety of genetic variants represented in a population or set of populations.
Mating between genetically related individuals.
Observations used to evaluate a population’s condition and response to an action.
The capacity for heritable variation to support responses to changing conditions.

A head count is only one measurement

A can recover numerically after a bottleneck while retaining reduced . Descendants multiply surviving allele copies; they do not automatically restore every lost variant. Population size and therefore answer different questions.

Small isolated populations may experience strong drift and increased mating among relatives. can increase homozygosity and expose effects of recessive alleles already present. It does not mean related individuals deliberately create new harmful alleles.

Connect a proposed action with its mechanism

A connection between habitats may permit movement and . If migrants reproduce, new alleles can enter a population and genetic differentiation may decline. Whether this happens depends on actual movement, survival and reproduction.

A population-management proposal should specify its biological mechanism and the evidence needed to evaluate it. Adding individuals, improving habitat and connecting populations are different interventions with potentially different effects.

The effects can include trade-offs. For example, introduced individuals may carry genetic variants suited to a different environment. An evidence-based evaluation considers both genetic contribution and the ecological setting rather than assuming that every transfer is beneficial.

Use cautious conclusions from limited data

Suppose a hypothetical monitoring report records more animals using a crossing structure and a rise in population size. That supports use of the structure and a demographic change. It does not alone establish increased gene flow or restored diversity at every locus.

Useful additional evidence might include successful breeding between populations, marker diversity, survival and the persistence of changes over generations. Sampling should be comparable across time.

Genetic diversity can support , but it is not a guarantee against extinction. Habitat, environmental change, population size and many other factors also matter.

Worked example

Evaluate a recovery claim

A population rises from 30 to 300 after a bottleneck. A report calls its original genetic diversity fully restored without genetic measurements.

  1. The head count supports numerical recovery.
  2. A bottleneck may have removed alleles that population growth alone cannot recover.
  3. Genetic measurements are needed to assess current diversity relative to earlier or comparison samples.
  4. The report’s genetic conclusion exceeds its demographic evidence.

Chapter review and final check

Can you distinguish a counted frequency, a model prediction and a causal explanation?

Learning goal

Integrate allele arithmetic, model assumptions and mechanisms of population change.

Before you begin

Identify the population, locus, denominator and assumptions before calculating.

Optional embedded reading

Chapter 19 · printed pp. 699–701

Open p. 699 · Open p. 701

Key terms: · · ·

Vocabulary help

Key terms

Words for this lesson

Use these definitions when you need help with a term.

The proportion of allele copies represented by a particular allele at a locus.
The proportion of individuals with a specified genotype.
A model in which allele frequencies remain constant and genotype frequencies follow p², 2pq and q² under stated conditions.
Random change in allele frequencies caused by chance sampling in finite populations.

How to complete this section

  1. Use the summary and synthesis example to find any mechanisms you need to revisit.
  2. Try the optional independent set before opening its feedback.
  3. Open the required final check and select Start. Correct six selections, save both written explanations, then select Submit and finish.
  4. Find earlier attempts and later practice in All My Work.

Expected work: one completed final-check run. The independent set and textbook review are optional.

Use the right method for the information

Genotype counts permit direct allele counting over 2N. Recessive phenotype information alone leaves some genotypes unknown, so a Hardy–Weinberg inference needs explicit assumptions. Expected genotype frequencies are p², 2pq and q² only within the model.

Keep frequencies distinct from counts. Multiply by population size only when an expected number is requested, and check that the complete categories total 1 or N as appropriate.

Interpret change without choosing a cause too soon

Selection links heritable variation with reproductive contribution; drift reflects chance; gene flow moves existing alleles between populations; mutation creates sequence variants. Non-random pairing can change genotype proportions without necessarily changing allele totals by itself.

A good population explanation uses the given evidence to distinguish these mechanisms. A small sample, an unexplained phenotype change or numerical recovery alone supports less than a complete claim about evolution or genetic diversity.

Connect the main ideas

TopicWhat you should be able to explain
Populations, gene pools and genetic variationDefine a gene pool and distinguish change in a population from change within an individual.
Allele frequencies and genotype frequenciesCalculate genotype and allele frequencies directly from diploid genotype counts.
The Hardy–Weinberg model and its assumptionsExplain the model’s conditions and distinguish allele totals from expected genotype frequencies.
Calculating expected genotype frequenciesSolve Hardy–Weinberg problems with explicit assumptions, separate quantities and reasonableness checks.
Using population data to test a predictionCompare observed and expected genotype counts without claiming that one mismatch identifies its cause.
Natural selection and non-random matingExplain selection through differential reproductive success and distinguish it from mate-pairing effects.
Genetic drift, bottlenecks and founder effectsDistinguish chance sampling from selection and compare bottleneck and founder cases.
Gene flow and mutationDistinguish movement of existing alleles from the creation of new sequence variants.
Genetic diversity and conservation evidenceUse population-genetic mechanisms to evaluate conservation evidence without assuming a universal outcome.

Worked example

Compare counts across population growth

Generation one has 16 aa individuals of 100 and generation two has 64 aa of 400. Assume the same complete-dominance Hardy–Weinberg model for both.

  1. The aa fractions are both 0.16.
  2. Under the stated model, q = 0.40 and p = 0.60 in both generations.
  3. Counts increased while inferred allele frequencies stayed equal.
  4. This supports no detected change at the studied locus under the assumptions.
  5. Without those assumptions, the recessive fractions alone would not determine every allele frequency.

Biotechnology and gene pools

How could a new trait spread, and what evidence would track it?

A hypothetical trait enters a breeding population

A hypothetical crop line carries an introduced allele. Nearby compatible plants can potentially receive pollen, but no offspring genotypes have yet been measured.

Pollen movement creates an opportunity for gene flow. Establishing inherited spread requires evidence that the pollen contributed to viable offspring and that the allele persists in the recipient population.

Separate movement, inheritance and consequences

A marker can track allele presence while reproductive data evaluate contribution. Frequency change over generations can be measured separately from the allele’s ecological effects.

This paper-based case does not assume that movement is always beneficial or always harmful. It asks what observations would support each specific biological claim.

  2. Type the term and check it. Capitalization and harmless punctuation do not matter; only reviewed aliases are accepted.
  3. The first incorrect attempt provides a cue. The second provides the answer and explanation.
  4. Complete the set and select Submit and finish.

Stop and reset asks for confirmation before clearing an unfinished run. Completed history is kept. Practice never increases required-check progress.

How to complete textbook practicechoose question → read → show your process → save

  3. Write or draw your response. Type your explanation in your own words. For a drawing, graph or table, work on paper and type the result and explanation here. Paper work is not stored by this course. Include labels, units and every required part. Use only supplied diagrams or data for analysis activities; do not perform the investigation procedures shown on a source page.

Core Vocabulary

Use each term to explain a relationship, not just repeat a definition.

How to use vocabulary and Frayer work
  1. Search the chapter terms or select a topic.
  2. Open a definition for its meaning, example and important distinction.
  3. Choose up to eight words for your Frayer work. Each chapter keeps a separate selection.
  4. Complete four responses per word, with 240 characters maximum per response.
  5. Select Collect this word. Editing it later returns it to draft status.
  6. After completing your own four valid responses, open the course model to compare. Print your work from All My Work.

Overlong Frayer text is not saved until shortened. No student answer is prefilled. Scientific accuracy is not automatically graded.
